title: Are English Departments in Decline?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles makes a data-backed case that many English departments' current teaching methods are failing students, built around his own "Points Make Prizes" technique for GCSE English reading questions, which reduces mark-scheme success to a simple, countable rule: the number of marks awarded equals the number of valid explanations offered, each grounded in a quote and beginning with a phrase like "this suggests." He supports the claim with a self-reported annual poll of over 1,000 students showing 31% jumped at least three grades from their mocks, plus a stream of student and parent testimonials, including one describing a school that threatened detention for students who used his method instead of the school's own. Salles argues teachers who dismiss a results-getting alternative method out of professional pride or discomfort are acting immorally, since a teacher's core responsibility is helping students achieve the best grades possible regardless of whose method produces them. He backs his broader claim of declining English instruction with Ofqual's National Reference Test, an unprepared-for annual assessment tracking whether year 11 students are genuinely improving in English, which has never prompted exam boards to award more top grades since 2017 and shows students at grades 3-6 specifically getting worse. His explanation is that overly complex classroom methods are slowing rather than accelerating student progress compared to students nine years earlier. He points readers to public School Performance Tables and the Family Fischer Trust's like-for-like school comparison tool as ways for any teacher, parent, or student to verify a school's actual track record before trusting its methods.
points: Distills a GCSE English reading-question mark scheme into one countable rule, the number of marks awarded equals the number of valid explanations grounded in a quote, based on rewriting hundreds of AQA-published answers in his own words to find the pattern.

Supports the claim with a self-reported annual poll of over 1,000 students showing 31% jumped at least three grades from their mocks using his method, alongside testimonials including a student rescued from grade 3 to grade 8.

Reports schools actively punishing students for using an alternative, results-producing method, including one that threatened detention, and argues this represents a moral failure of teachers' core responsibility to students' outcomes.

Cites Ofqual's unprepared-for National Reference Test, run annually since 2017, as objective evidence that English attainment for grades 3-6 students has been declining rather than improving under current classroom methods.

Directs readers to public accountability tools, government School Performance Tables and the Family Fischer Trust's like-for-like school comparison site, as ways to verify a school's or teacher's actual track record before trusting their approach.
quotes: That's over 1000 students who have replied. 31% of my viewers say they went up at least 3 grades from their mocks. There isn't a teacher or English team in the country that can claim that.

Shockingly at one point his school said they would put him in detention if he did not use the school's method! We ignored the school. I was equally horrified to learn recently another nearby school has told its children that your method is fake/false and not to follow it.
You can't dismiss an approach just because you don't like it, as a teacher it is your responsibility, your moral purpose, to help your students to get the best grades that they can.
I read every single answer ever published by AQA. Hundreds of them. And then I rewrote each one in my own words, to work out what made the difference between grades.
Only Ofqual has never told the exam boards to award more English grades at 4-9. Why? Because since 2017, English has been getting worse.

Students at grades 3, 4, 5 and 6 are getting worse, because the methods they are taught in school don't make sense. They are spending so much time learning these complex methods that they are actually making much slower progress than students 9 years ago.
